chapters.title: Strategy Evaluation and Strategic Control
chapters.summary: Evaluating whether a strategy is working: operational versus strategic control, the four types of strategic control (premise, surveillance, special alert, implementation), Rumelt's criteria and Balanced Scorecard basics.

lesson.heading: Why strategic control
lesson.body:
Strategies are built on assumptions about an uncertain future. **Strategy evaluation** checks whether the strategy is being implemented as planned and whether it is still the right strategy. **Strategic control** is the continuous process of tracking strategy as it is implemented, detecting problems or changes in its premises, and making adjustments.

| Operational control | Strategic control |
| --- | --- |
| Checks efficiency of day-to-day activities against budgets and standards | Checks whether the strategy and its assumptions remain valid |
| Short term, internal | Long term, external and internal |
| Done by middle and lower management | Done by top management |
| Asks: are we doing things right? | Asks: are we still doing the right things? |

The basic control process: set standards, measure actual performance, compare and analyse deviations, take corrective action.

lesson.heading: Types of strategic control
lesson.body:
| Type | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Premise control | Systematically checks whether the planning **premises** (assumptions about environment and industry) still hold | A plan assumed the rupee at a certain rate; treasury tracks it monthly |
| Strategic surveillance | **Unfocused, broad** monitoring of internal and external events for anything that may affect strategy | Managers scan news, trade journals, social media, competitor launches |
| Special alert control | **Rapid, thorough rethink** of strategy after a sudden, unexpected event | Crisis team after a plant fire, pandemic or sudden ban |
| Implementation control | Checks whether strategic thrusts and **milestones** are achieved, and whether the strategy should change in light of results | Review at the end of each project phase |

Premise control is **focused** on specific assumptions. Strategic surveillance is **unfocused** and wide. Implementation control works through monitoring strategic thrusts (key projects) and milestone reviews.

lesson.heading: Evaluation criteria and the Balanced Scorecard
lesson.body:
Richard Rumelt suggested four criteria to evaluate a strategy:

- **Consistency:** goals and policies are not mutually inconsistent.
- **Consonance:** the strategy adapts to the external environment and its changes.
- **Advantage:** it creates or maintains a competitive advantage.
- **Feasibility:** it can be implemented with available resources and does not create unsolvable sub-problems.

The **Balanced Scorecard** (Robert Kaplan and David Norton) translates strategy into measures across four perspectives, so that managers do not rely on financial results alone:

| Perspective | Question | Sample measures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Financial | How do we look to shareholders? | ROCE, revenue growth, EVA |
| Customer | How do customers see us? | Market share, retention, satisfaction score |
| Internal business process | What must we excel at? | Cycle time, defect rate, on-time delivery |
| Learning and growth | Can we continue to improve and create value? | Training hours, employee retention, new product ideas |

The scorecard mixes lagging (financial) and leading (learning, process) indicators.

lesson.heading: Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Calling budget variance analysis 'strategic control'. It is operational control.
- Mixing up premise control (specific assumptions) with strategic surveillance (broad, unfocused monitoring).
- Using special alert control for gradual trends. It is for sudden, high-impact events.
- In the Balanced Scorecard, placing employee training under internal process. It belongs to learning and growth.
- In case answers, naming the control without quoting the case fact that shows it.

keyPoints: Operational control = efficiency of routine activities; strategic control = validity of strategy and its premises.
Premise control: focused check of planning assumptions.
Strategic surveillance: broad, unfocused monitoring of events.
Special alert control: rapid rethink after a sudden, unexpected event.
Implementation control: strategic thrusts and milestone reviews.
Rumelt's criteria: consistency, consonance, advantage, feasibility.
Balanced Scorecard: financial, customer, internal business process, learning and growth.

cases.title: Case: SkyNest Hotels Ltd
cases.body:
SkyNest Hotels Ltd prepared a five-year plan to open 30 mid-priced hotels in pilgrimage towns. The plan assumed that domestic religious tourism would grow at about 12% a year and that a proposed regional airport near two key towns would open by 2027.

The strategy cell receives a monthly report tracking pilgrim footfall data and the progress of the airport project. In addition, all general managers are asked to share anything they notice in local news, social media or competitor activity that could affect the business, even if it seems unrelated.

The plan is divided into phases; at the end of each phase the board reviews whether the hotels opened so far are meeting occupancy targets before releasing funds for the next phase.

In 2026, a flash flood damaged roads to one major pilgrimage town. Within 48 hours the CEO convened a crisis team that re-examined the expansion plan for the entire region.

The board now also wants to track guest satisfaction scores, average check-in time, staff training hours and return on capital employed in one report.

questions.prompt: The monthly report tracking pilgrim footfall and progress of the airport project is an example of:
questions.explanation: The plan was based on two specific assumptions (12% tourism growth, airport by 2027). A focused, systematic check of whether these planning premises still hold is premise control.

questions.prompt: Asking general managers to report anything in news, social media or competitor activity that could affect the business is:
questions.explanation: This is broad, unfocused monitoring of a wide range of events inside and outside the firm, which is strategic surveillance.

questions.prompt: In the Balanced Scorecard, 'average check-in time' falls under which perspective?
questions.explanation: Check-in time measures the efficiency of an internal operating process. Guest satisfaction is a customer measure, training hours a learning and growth measure, ROCE a financial measure.

questions.prompt: In the given case, identify and explain the four types of strategic control used by SkyNest Hotels Ltd.
questions.answer:
- **Premise control:** the monthly report on pilgrim footfall and airport progress checks the two planning assumptions (12% growth, airport by 2027). It is a focused, systematic check of whether the premises still hold.
- **Strategic surveillance:** general managers report anything relevant from news, social media or competitors. It is broad, unfocused monitoring that can pick up threats premise control would miss.
- **Implementation control:** the board reviews occupancy at the end of each phase before releasing funds. These are milestone reviews that check whether the strategy is on track and whether it should continue.
- **Special alert control:** after the flash flood, a crisis team met within 48 hours to rethink the regional plan. This is a rapid, thorough reconsideration of strategy after a sudden, unexpected event.

Together these controls let SkyNest adjust a long-term plan as the uncertain future unfolds.

questions.prompt: In the given case, identify and explain how the board's proposed single report reflects the Balanced Scorecard.
questions.answer:
The Balanced Scorecard (Kaplan and Norton) measures performance from four perspectives, so managers do not rely only on financial results. The board's report covers all four:

| Measure in case | Perspective | Question answered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Return on capital employed | Financial | How do we look to shareholders? |
| Guest satisfaction scores | Customer | How do customers see us? |
| Average check-in time | Internal business process | What must we excel at? |
| Staff training hours | Learning and growth | Can we keep improving? |

Training and process measures are leading indicators. Customer and financial measures are lagging outcomes. One report links SkyNest's expansion strategy to day-to-day measures and gives a balanced view of performance.

questions.prompt: Which criterion in Rumelt's framework asks whether the strategy represents an adaptive response to the external environment?
questions.explanation: Consonance checks fit with the environment and its changes. Consistency checks internal coherence, advantage checks competitive edge and feasibility checks resource adequacy.

questions.prompt: Comparing actual material cost with standard cost every week is an example of:
questions.explanation: Measuring efficiency of routine activities against standards and budgets is operational control. It does not question the strategy or its assumptions.

questions.prompt: Implementation control is typically carried out through:
options: Monitoring strategic thrusts and milestone reviews
questions.explanation: Implementation control tracks key projects (strategic thrusts) and reviews at milestones whether the strategy is working and should continue as planned.

questions.prompt: 'Employee retention rate' in a Balanced Scorecard belongs to the:
questions.explanation: Learning and growth covers people, information systems and organisational capability: training, skills, retention, employee satisfaction.

questions.prompt: Strategic surveillance is designed to be focused on a few specific planning assumptions.
questions.explanation: That describes premise control. Strategic surveillance is deliberately broad and unfocused to catch unanticipated events.

questions.prompt: The Balanced Scorecard combines financial measures with non-financial measures of performance.
questions.explanation: Financial measures are lagging. The scorecard adds customer, internal process and learning and growth measures that drive future financial results.

questions.prompt: Select Richard Rumelt's criteria for evaluating a strategy.
questions.explanation: Rumelt's four criteria are consistency, consonance, advantage and feasibility. Profitability is an outcome, not one of his criteria.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: The type of strategic control triggered by a sudden, unexpected event that requires a rapid reconsideration of strategy is called special ___ control.
questions.explanation: Special alert control is often run by a crisis team. Examples: a natural disaster, a sudden government ban, a product recall or the failure of a key supplier.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between operational control and strategic control.
questions.answer:
- **Purpose:** operational control checks the efficiency of routine activities. Strategic control checks whether the strategy is being implemented as planned and whether its premises are still valid.
- **Focus:** operational control is internal. Strategic control looks at both the external environment and internal performance.
- **Time frame:** operational control is short term (daily, weekly, monthly). Strategic control is long term and continuous.
- **Level:** operational control is done by middle and lower management. Strategic control is done by top management.
- **Tools:** operational control uses budgets, standard costing and variance analysis. Strategic control uses premise control, surveillance, special alert and implementation control.

Both are needed: efficient operations add little value if the strategy itself is outdated.

questions.prompt: Explain the process of strategy evaluation and control.
questions.answer:
- **Set standards:** derive performance standards from strategic objectives, both quantitative (ROCE, market share) and qualitative (brand image, employee morale).
- **Measure actual performance:** collect timely and reliable data, financial and non-financial.
- **Compare and analyse deviations:** find significant variances and their causes, whether internal (poor execution) or external (changed premises).
- **Take corrective action:** improve implementation, revise objectives or standards, or reformulate the strategy itself.

The process is continuous and feeds back into strategy formulation. Its effectiveness depends on top management support, an information system and the willingness to change course.

chapters.title: Contemporary Themes: Digital and Sustainable Strategy
chapters.summary: Applying the syllabus frameworks to digital transformation, platform business models, sustainability, the triple bottom line and shared value, as these themes appear in case scenarios across the paper.

lesson.heading: How this chapter fits the syllabus
lesson.body:
The ICAI new scheme Strategic Management syllabus has five chapters: Introduction to Strategic Management, Strategic Analysis: External Environment, Strategic Analysis: Internal Environment, Strategic Choices, and Strategy Implementation and Evaluation. Digital and sustainability themes are not a separate examinable chapter. They appear as the **setting of case scenarios** (an EV maker, an e-commerce platform, a green packaging firm).

This chapter shows how to apply the frameworks you already know to such cases: PESTLE and five forces for digital disruption, VRIO and the value chain for data and platform assets, Ansoff and generic strategies for green products, and Lewin and culture for digital transformation. Check the latest ICAI study material for any new content added for your attempt.

lesson.heading: Digital strategy and transformation
lesson.body:
**Digital transformation** is the use of digital technologies (cloud, mobile, data analytics, AI, automation) to change how a firm creates and delivers value. It is a strategic change, not only an IT project.

| Framework | Digital lens |
| --- | --- |
| PESTLE | Technological factor (AI, digital payments); legal factor (data protection rules) |
| Five forces | Digital platforms lower entry barriers and raise buyer power through price transparency; apps can be substitutes |
| Value chain | Digitised marketing and sales, data-driven operations, e-procurement, online service |
| VRIO | Proprietary customer data and algorithms can be valuable, rare and hard to imitate if organised well |
| Implementation | Needs new skills, agile structures, a culture of experimentation and change management |

**Platform business models** connect two or more user groups (buyers and sellers, riders and drivers). They benefit from **network effects**: each additional user makes the platform more valuable to others, which can create winner-take-most markets.

Digital strategy should start from the business strategy: a cost leader uses digital tools for efficiency, a differentiator for personalised customer experience.

lesson.heading: Sustainability and strategy
lesson.body:
**Sustainable strategy** pursues long-term business success while meeting environmental, social and governance (ESG) expectations.

- **Triple bottom line** (John Elkington): judge performance on **people** (social), **planet** (environmental) and **profit** (economic).
- **Stakeholder approach:** consider employees, customers, suppliers, communities, regulators and investors, not only shareholders.
- **Creating shared value** (Michael Porter and Mark Kramer): find business opportunities in social problems, for example by reconceiving products for underserved markets, redefining productivity in the value chain (less energy, water, waste) and building local supplier clusters.
- **Circular economy:** design products for reuse, repair and recycling instead of take-make-dispose.

Sustainability can support a **differentiation** strategy (green brand, premium) or a **cost** strategy (energy and waste savings). **Greenwashing**, which means claiming environmental benefits that are not real, damages reputation and can attract regulatory action.

lesson.heading: Answering case questions on these themes
lesson.body:
Worked approach for 'In the given case, identify and explain how sustainability gives the firm a competitive advantage':

- Name the framework (generic strategy, VRIO or value chain).
- Quote the case fact (for example, 'solar power cuts energy cost by 30%').
- Link it to the advantage (lower cost in operations -> cost advantage; eco-label valued by customers -> differentiation).
- Note sustainability of the advantage (can rivals copy it easily?).

**Common mistakes:** treating sustainability as only CSR spending, unrelated to strategy; claiming every digital tool is a core competence; ignoring the people and culture side of digital transformation; recommending a platform model without network effects or scale.

keyPoints: ICAI new scheme SM has five chapters; digital and sustainability themes appear as case settings, applied through the standard frameworks.
Digital transformation = strategic change using digital technology; needs skills, structure and culture change.
Platforms connect user groups; network effects make each additional user add value for others.
Triple bottom line: people, planet, profit.
Creating shared value (Porter and Kramer): reconceive products and markets, redefine value chain productivity, build local clusters.
Sustainability can support cost (efficiency) or differentiation (green brand); greenwashing destroys trust.
Circular economy: reuse, repair, recycle instead of take-make-dispose.

cases.title: Case: KisanKart Agritech Pvt Ltd
cases.body:
KisanKart runs a mobile app that connects 4.5 lakh farmers in Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh with buyers such as food processors and wholesalers. As more farmers join, more buyers join because supply is assured; more buyers in turn attract more farmers with better prices. The firm owns no warehouses; storage and transport are provided by partner firms coordinated through the app.

KisanKart has built a database of soil, weather and price data over seven years and uses its own crop-advisory algorithm, which farmers say has raised yields by about 18%. Competitors have copied the app's features but cannot match the depth of data.

KisanKart also runs a programme that trains women farmers in organic methods and buys their produce at an assured price for a premium organic brand sold in metro cities. Its packaging is made from crop residue, which reduces stubble burning. Investors now ask KisanKart to report on social and environmental impact along with profit.

The founders are converting the firm's paper-based procurement team to fully digital processes, but many older field staff are anxious and some have resisted using tablets.

questions.prompt: The way more farmers attract more buyers and more buyers attract more farmers on KisanKart is an example of:
questions.explanation: On a platform, each additional user on one side increases the value for users on the other side. That self-reinforcing loop is a network effect.

questions.prompt: An agritech firm owns no warehouses or trucks; storage and transport are provided by partner firms that it coordinates through its app. Its organisation is closest to a:
questions.explanation: A core firm that coordinates outsourced partners through contracts and IT, while keeping only key activities in-house, has a network structure.

questions.prompt: Investors asking KisanKart to report social and environmental impact along with profit reflects the concept of:
questions.explanation: Reporting on people (social), planet (environmental) and profit (economic) is the triple bottom line.

questions.prompt: In the given case, identify and explain whether KisanKart's data and crop-advisory algorithm give it a sustained competitive advantage, using the VRIO framework.
questions.answer:
- **Valuable:** yes. The advisory raises farmers' yields by about 18%, which attracts and retains farmers and so feeds the platform's network effects.
- **Rare:** yes. Seven years of soil, weather and price data across two States is held by KisanKart alone.
- **Inimitable:** yes. Competitors copied app features but cannot match the depth of data. The data is path dependent (built over time), and the algorithm is proprietary.
- **Organised:** yes. The firm already uses the data actively in its advisory service and app.

The data assets pass all four tests and give a **sustained competitive advantage**. In contrast, the app features are valuable but imitable, so they gave only a temporary advantage. KisanKart should keep investing in data quality and protect it through security and privacy compliance.

questions.prompt: In the given case, identify and explain how KisanKart creates shared value through its sustainability initiatives.
questions.answer:
Creating shared value (Porter and Kramer) means pursuing business opportunities that also solve social problems.

- **Reconceiving products and markets:** the premium organic brand for metro cities creates a new profitable product line built on organic produce from trained women farmers.
- **Redefining productivity in the value chain:** packaging made from crop residue gives the firm a low-cost input and also reduces stubble burning and air pollution.
- **Enabling local cluster development:** training women farmers and buying at assured prices builds a reliable, skilled local supplier base and raises rural incomes.

These initiatives are part of the business model, not separate charity. They strengthen supply security and brand differentiation while delivering social and environmental benefits.

questions.prompt: In the given case, identify and explain how KisanKart should manage the resistance to digitising its procurement team.
questions.answer:
Older field staff are anxious about tablets: resistance arising from fear of the unknown, loss of competence and job insecurity. Using Lewin's model:

- **Unfreezing:** explain why digital procurement is needed (speed, accuracy, better prices for farmers), reassure staff about job security, and involve respected senior staff as champions.
- **Changing:** give hands-on training in local languages, provide simple interfaces, pilot with volunteers, pair older staff with digitally skilled colleagues, and offer support helplines.
- **Refreezing:** recognise and reward adoption, update procedures so paper forms are retired, and track usage.

Digital transformation succeeds only when people, skills and culture change along with technology.

questions.prompt: Making false or exaggerated claims about a product's environmental benefits is called:
questions.explanation: Greenwashing misleads stakeholders about environmental performance. When exposed, it damages reputation and can attract regulatory action.

questions.prompt: Under Porter's five forces, online price-comparison websites in a retail industry most directly:
options: Increase the bargaining power of buyers
Increase the bargaining power of suppliers
questions.explanation: Price transparency lowers buyers' search costs and lets them switch easily, which increases buyer power and usually intensifies price rivalry.

questions.prompt: A firm installs rooftop solar power and water recycling at its plants, cutting its operating costs below rivals. Which generic strategy does this sustainability initiative mainly support?
questions.explanation: Lower energy and water costs reduce unit cost, supporting a cost advantage. If customers paid a premium for the green image, it would support differentiation instead.

questions.prompt: Digital transformation is purely a technology project and does not require changes in culture or skills.
questions.explanation: Digital transformation changes how value is created. It needs new skills, structures, processes and a culture open to experimentation, so it is a strategic change managed by top leadership.

questions.prompt: Under a circular economy approach, products are designed for reuse, repair and recycling.
questions.explanation: The circular economy replaces the linear take-make-dispose model by keeping materials in use as long as possible.

questions.prompt: Select the three dimensions of the triple bottom line.
questions.explanation: John Elkington's triple bottom line judges performance on social (people), environmental (planet) and economic (profit) outcomes. Price and promotion are marketing mix elements.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: When each additional user makes a platform more valuable to other users, the platform benefits from network ___.
questions.explanation: Network effects create self-reinforcing growth and can make markets winner-take-most, which raises entry barriers for late entrants.

questions.prompt: Explain how digital technologies can change a firm's value chain, with examples.
questions.answer:
- **Inbound logistics:** IoT tracking of shipments and automated stock replenishment.
- **Operations:** automation, robotics and predictive maintenance using sensor data.
- **Outbound logistics:** route optimisation and real-time delivery tracking.
- **Marketing and sales:** digital channels, personalised offers from customer data, e-commerce.
- **Service:** chatbots, remote diagnostics and self-service portals.
- **Support activities:** e-procurement, cloud ERP, digital HR (online learning, analytics), R&D using simulation and AI.

Digitising activities can lower cost (cost leadership) or improve customer experience (differentiation), and it improves linkages because data flows across activities. The firm should digitise activities that support its business strategy, not adopt technology for its own sake.

questions.prompt: Explain how sustainability can be a source of competitive advantage rather than only a cost.
questions.answer:
- **Cost advantage:** energy efficiency, waste reduction, recycling and water savings lower operating cost.
- **Differentiation:** eco-friendly products and transparent sourcing attract customers willing to pay a premium.
- **Access to capital:** investors increasingly prefer firms with good ESG performance, lowering the cost of capital.
- **Risk reduction:** anticipating environmental regulation and resource scarcity avoids future disruption (premise control on environmental assumptions).
- **Talent:** a credible purpose helps attract and retain employees.
- **Innovation:** constraints push new products and business models, such as circular products.

The advantage lasts only if initiatives are genuine and built into the business model. Greenwashing or token CSR gives no lasting advantage.
